title: The Symbol of the Faith
subtitle: The original Nicene Creed, ratified by the Council of Nicaea in 325
source: Schaff & Wace, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series II, Vol. 14: The Seven Ecumenical Councils (Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 1900). Public domain. Source text via Wikisource.

sections.title: On the Symbol of the Faith
sections.framing: The Creed below is the original Symbol set forth by the 318 Fathers at Nicaea in 325. It is the first half of the Creed every Orthodox Christian still recites at the Divine Liturgy. The article on the Holy Spirit was filled out, and the closing articles on the Church, baptism, the resurrection, and the age to come were added, at the Second Ecumenical Council at Constantinople in 381, what we now know together as the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed. The anathemas in the final sentence are the Council's formal condemnation of the principal Arian formulae. They are not recited in the Liturgy but were dogmatic at the time of issue and remain so.
paragraphs: The text below is preserved in the Acts of the Ecumenical Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon, in the Epistle of Eusebius of Caesarea to his own Church, in the Epistle of St. Athanasius to the Emperor Jovian, in the Ecclesiastical Histories of Theodoret and Socrates, and elsewhere. The variations among the witnesses are negligible.

sections.title: The Ecthesis of the Synod at Nice
sections.citation: The Symbol set forth by the 318 Holy Fathers, 325 A.D.
paragraphs: We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the only-begotten of his Father, of the substance of the Father, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten (γεννηθέντα), not made, being of one substance (ὁμοούσιον, consubstantialem) with the Father. By whom all things were made, both which be in heaven and in earth. Who for us men and for our salvation came down from heaven and was incarnate and was made man. He suffered and the third day he rose again, and ascended into heaven. And he shall come again to judge both the quick and the dead. And we believe in the Holy Ghost.

And whosoever shall say that there was a time when the Son of God was not (ἤν ποτε ὅτε οὐκ ἦν), or that before he was begotten he was not, or that he was made of things that were not, or that he is of a different substance or essence from the Father, or that he is a creature, or subject to change or conversion — all that so say, the Catholic and Apostolic Church anathematizes them.
notes: ὁμοούσιον (homoousion), "consubstantial" or "of one substance" with the Father. The decisive word at Nicaea. The Arians could equivocate around the softer formula "of like substance" (ὁμοιούσιον, homoiousion, separated from the Nicene word by a single iota), but the homoousion they could not subscribe to without abandoning their position. The same word is rendered consubstantial in the liturgical English used today and of one essence in the older Hapgood-tradition translation.

"There was a time when the Son of God was not" (ἤν ποτε ὅτε οὐκ ἦν) is the Arian slogan being condemned: that the Son is a creature, the first and highest, but not eternal. The Council answers that He is begotten eternally of the Father, not made.

The article on the Holy Spirit ends abruptly here because the question would not be pressed until the Macedonian / Pneumatomachian controversy of the 360s and 370s; the Second Council at Constantinople in 381 supplied the full pneumatological article we recite today.

sections.title: An earlier proposal: the Creed of Eusebius of Caesarea
sections.framing: Eusebius of Caesarea, the church historian, who had been under suspicion of leanings toward Arius, presented to the council the baptismal creed of his own see as evidence of his own orthodoxy. His own letter to his diocese (preserved by St. Athanasius and Theodoret) reports that the Fathers accepted his protestation and then, with the addition of certain phrases, principally consubstantial with the Father, issued the Symbol above. The standard reading sees Eusebius's account as apologetic; the Fathers did not so much adopt his creed as look past it, choosing the stronger language of homoousios, which the Arians could not equivocate around, as the formula of the Faith. The Eusebian text is preserved here as the baptismal creed of fourth-century Caesarea and as one of the documentary witnesses to the deliberations at Nicaea.
sections.citation: From Eusebius's own Epistle to his diocese; preserved in St. Athanasius and Theodoret.
paragraphs: We believe in one only God, Father Almighty, Creator of things visible and invisible; and in the Lord Jesus Christ, for he is the Word of God, God of God, Light of Light, life of life, his only Son, the first-born of all creatures, begotten of the Father before all time, by whom also everything was created, who became flesh for our redemption, who lived and suffered amongst men, rose again the third day, returned to the Father, and will come again one day in his glory to judge the quick and the dead. We believe also in the Holy Ghost. We believe that each of these three is and subsists; the Father truly as Father, the Son truly as Son, the Holy Ghost truly as Holy Ghost; as our Lord also said, when he sent his disciples to preach: Go and teach all nations, and baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
